bp: A blockchain transaction does not jump straight from a user's wallet into a permanent block. First it waits in a public waiting room, usually called the mempool: the set of pending transactions that network participants have heard about but that miners or block builders have not yet written into the chain. This paper studies whether that waiting room can be used as a witness against unfair miners. The ordinary concern is simple. A miner might censor a transaction by refusing to include it, or displace it by changing the expected order so another transaction wins the timing advantage. Large blockchains such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Cardano have not adopted many proposed defenses against this manipulation. Users therefore rely on practical monitoring services such as Mempool.space, which compare what different observers saw. The paper asks a first-principles question: when observers disagree, is that evidence of miner misconduct, or just evidence that messages reached different machines at different times?
wh: The hard part is that the mempool is not one shared object sitting in one place. Each observer has a local view formed by network messages arriving over time. If observer A saw a transaction and observer B did not, that difference may mean a miner or relay path suppressed the transaction. It may also mean B has not received the message yet. The same difficulty appears with transaction displacement. Two transactions can be sent close together, spread through the network along different routes, and reach observers in different orders even if nobody is cheating. A simple audit must therefore separate hostile absence from ordinary delay. The abstract reports that this separation can fail badly: mempool auditing can mis-accuse miners with probability larger than 25 percent in some settings. The tension is speed versus confidence. If the auditor accuses quickly, normal propagation noise looks like an attack. If it waits too long, the attack signal becomes less useful for real-time protection.
naive: A smart beginner would place observers around the network, record every pending transaction they see, and accuse a miner whenever the miner's block contradicts that shared record. If most observers saw transaction X before transaction Y, then X should come first; if observers saw X and the miner skipped it, call that censorship. This fails because there is no perfect shared record. Observers do not receive the same messages at the same instant, and the abstract's result says those discrepancies are large enough to create more than 25 percent false accusations in some cases. The naive rule treats every mismatch as intent, when many mismatches are just the cost of moving messages through a distributed network.
ap: The paper's core move is to analyze auditing as a timing and agreement problem, not as a simple yes-or-no comparison. It studies the interplay between what mempool observers see and what can legitimately be concluded about malicious miners in Bitcoin and Ethereum. Instead of assuming that observer disagreement directly proves censorship or displacement, it asks what conditions make the observers' record reliable enough to support an accusation. The positive result gives a concrete boundary. Auditing can successfully check the execution of any two transactions with overwhelming probability, reported as 99.9 percent, when two things are true: all observers consistently receive both transactions, and the transactions are sent at least 30 seconds apart. That turns mempool auditing from an informal practice into a measured instrument. It can be strong when transactions have enough time separation and shared visibility, but weak when transactions arrive in a burst or appear unevenly across observers.
mech: The mechanism begins with transactions moving through Bitcoin or Ethereum before they are mined. The inputs are the transactions themselves, their send times, the local mempool records collected by observers, and the block later produced by a miner. First, observers record whether and when they received each transaction. Second, the audit compares these local records across observers. A transaction consistently received by all observers is a stronger witness than one seen only by a few, because shared receipt reduces the chance that a later absence is merely a visibility problem. Third, for a pair of transactions, the audit looks at their separation in time. If they were sent very close together, differences in network travel time can easily reverse or blur their apparent order. If they were sent at least 30 seconds apart, the abstract says the observers' evidence becomes reliable enough to audit their execution with 99.9 percent probability, provided both were consistently received. Fourth, the audit compares this observer-based expectation with the miner's actual block behavior: whether the miner included, skipped, or displaced the transactions. The output is not a blanket guilty-or-innocent verdict for every transaction. It is a conditional judgment: accusations are meaningful only where observer agreement and time spacing make normal network delay an unlikely explanation.
math: The main mathematical ideas are probability, timing thresholds, and error measurement. Probability is needed because the auditor never sees a miner's private intention. It only sees traces: which observers received which pending transactions, when they received them, and how the mined block treated those transactions. From those traces, the auditor estimates how likely a mismatch is under normal network behavior versus malicious behavior. Error measurement asks how often the audit would accuse an honest miner. The abstract's larger-than-25-percent mis-accusation result is a false-positive warning: the measurement process can turn harmless disagreement into blame. The 30-second condition is a threshold, a chosen boundary where enough time has passed that ordinary propagation differences should have mostly settled. The 99.9 percent figure is not magic certainty; it is a statement that under the paper's stated conditions, repeated audits of two consistently received, well-separated transactions should almost always reach the right execution judgment. The tradeoff is speed versus reliability. Short waiting windows preserve immediacy but confuse delay with manipulation. Longer separations produce cleaner evidence but apply only to the subset of transaction pairs that naturally meet that timing condition.
dots: This paper sits in the repo's blockchain transaction security thread with work on transaction fee mechanisms and validator selfish mining. Those papers share a deeper object: a public ledger whose formal rules can still leave room for unfair timing, hidden bargains, or selective inclusion. The fee-mechanism paper asks how to design the auction for scarce block space so miner-user side deals are deterred. The Polkadot selfish-mining paper asks how future role information lets validators profit by delaying valid blocks. This mempool auditing paper asks a complementary question: if manipulation may happen, when can outside observers detect it without blaming normal delay? It also connects to the repo's DNS manipulation measurement paper, where dynamic network behavior makes censorship detection hard, and to the information concept, where surprise or disagreement is useful only after ordinary sources of noise have been accounted for.
ww: The approach works when it respects what the observers can and cannot know. A single local mempool record is too fragile because it may reflect only one path through the network. Comparing many observers helps because agreement across independent viewpoints is stronger evidence than one machine's memory. Time separation helps for a different reason: it gives the network enough room to deliver the earlier transaction widely before the later one becomes relevant. When all observers consistently receive two transactions and the transactions are at least 30 seconds apart, a later inconsistency in execution is less likely to be explained by harmless propagation lag. That is why the paper can report 99.9 percent successful auditing under those conditions. The same reasoning explains the negative result. When transactions are close together or observer views are uneven, the audit is trying to infer intent from evidence that has not stabilized. In that regime, the mechanism can produce confident-looking accusations that are mathematically unsupported.
po: The payoff is a clearer boundary around a practice blockchain users already rely on. Mempool auditing is not dismissed as useless, but it is not treated as a universal fairness detector either. The paper shows that in some settings it can falsely accuse miners with probability above 25 percent, which is too high for a trustworthy blame system. It also shows a strong positive case: two transactions can be audited with 99.9 percent probability when all observers receive them and their send times are at least 30 seconds apart. That result explains why batch-order fair-ordering schemes offer strong guarantees only for a limited subset of real deployments.
limits: The claims depend on the observer model, the Bitcoin and Ethereum settings analyzed, and the condition that transactions are consistently received by all observers. The abstract does not say that every observer placement, network load pattern, miner strategy, or blockchain protocol will have the same error rates. The 99.9 percent result applies to pairs of transactions at least 30 seconds apart, so it does not cover crowded bursts where ordering conflicts are often most valuable. The work also audits evidence of execution; it cannot directly read miner intent. A mismatch may support an accusation only after ordinary delay and uneven visibility have been ruled out by the paper's conditions.
